## Deep learning-based power transformer condition monitoring and fault diagnosis algorithm

## Wei Chen

State Grid Gansu Electric Power Company,

Lanzhou, 730030, China Email: persai2707@sina.com

Abstract: Power  transformers  are  critical  in  smart  grids,  but  accurate  fault diagnosis remains challenging due to limitations in conventional dissolved gas analysis  and  data-intensive  deep  learning  methods.  This  paper  introduces  an integrated deep learning framework combining convolutional neural networks with bidirectional long short-term memory via an adaptive multi-head attention mechanism.  The  model  jointly  processes  dissolved  gas  analysis  profiles  and vibration signatures: convolutional layers extract spatial features from gas data, while  bidirectional  units  capture  temporal  vibration  dynamics.  The  attention mechanism  dynamically  highlights  discriminative  features,  improving  both interpretability  and  accuracy.  Evaluated  on  the  IEC  dissolved  gas  analysis dataset  and  real  vibration  records,  our  method  achieves  98.2%  diagnostic accuracy, surpassing support vector machines (85.1%) and deep belief networks  (90.8%).  Additional  tests  confirm  robustness  in  detecting  incipient faults  under  varied  conditions.  Attention  weights  align  with  known  failure mechanisms, offering a reliable, interpretable tool for predictive maintenance.

Keywords: power  transformers;  fault  diagnosis;  deep  learning;  dissolved  gas analysis; DGA; attention mechanism.

Reference to  this  paper  should  be  made  as  follows:  Chen,  W.  (2026)  'Deep learning-based  power  transformer  condition  monitoring  and  fault  diagnosis algorithm', Int.  J.  Information  and  Communication  Technology ,  Vol.  27, No. 17, pp.35-51.

Biographical notes: Wei Chen is the Deputy Senior Engineer at the State Grid Gansu Electric Power Company. He obtained a Bachelor's degree in Electrical Engineering  and  Automation  from  Chongqing  University  (June  2007).  He published  one  EI-index  journal  paper.  His  research  interests  include  current transformer equipment, transformers and high voltage tests.

## 1 Introduction

As the core hub equipment of power grids, the operational status of power transformers directly impacts the safety and stability of the entire power system (Wang et al., 2016). Within the architecture of smart grids, transformers serve not only as critical nodes for voltage transformation but also as hubs enabling bidirectional energy flow, cyber-physical  integration,  and  flexible  system  regulation.  Their  condition  is  directly linked  to  regional  power  supply  reliability,  renewable  energy  integration  capacity,  and the overall resilience of the grid. Statistics indicate that mechanical vibration accounts for over 60%  of transformer failures (Kornatowski and Eugeniusz, 2012). Internal mechanical defects such as winding deformation and core loosening are often triggered by operational conditions like short-circuit current impacts and prolonged electrodynamic forces (Zhang et al., 2014). These defects are characterised by strong concealment, slow progression,  and  severe  consequences.  Traditional  fault  diagnosis  primarily  relies  on dissolved gas analysis (DGA) in transformer oil (Su and Mi, 2000). This method analyses the concentration and ratios of characteristic gases like hydrogen, methane, and acetylene to infer fault types. Although DGA is a mature technology, it remains fundamentally an indirect  diagnostic method with significant limitations: This technique has been widely adopted  in  industry  since  the  mid-20th  century  and  has  led  to  the  establishment  of international standards such as IEC 60599 and IEEE C57.104. Its decades-long practice has accumulated a rich corpus of fault cases and empirical knowledge, solidifying its role as a benchmark in the field. On one hand, it lacks sensitivity to early-stage mechanical defects,  making  early  fault  warning  challenging  (King,  1982).  On  the  other  hand, diagnostic outcomes heavily depend on the experience of maintenance personnel and are susceptible  to  interference  from  factors  like  equipment  model  (Starcke  et  al.,  2011), operational  history,  and  oil  characteristics,  resulting  in  high  false  alarm  and  missed detection  rates  (Xiaojun  et  al.,  2010).  Furthermore,  DGA  data  alone  is  insufficient  for precise fault localisation, failing to meet the urgent demands of modern smart grids for accurate  equipment  condition  monitoring  and  predictive  maintenance  (Duchowski  and Mannebach,  2006).  Despite  its  limitations,  DGA  has  endured  due  to  its  non-invasive sampling  nature,  well-understood  mechanisms  of  fault  gas  generation,  and  globally accepted  standardised  ratio  criteria.  These  attributes  made  it  an  indispensable  and practical  primary  diagnostic  tool  during  the  long  period  before  superior  alternatives emerged.

Artificial intelligence technologies, exemplified by deep learning, have injected new momentum into transformer condition monitoring (Vidiyala et al., 2025). For instance, deep learning-based image recognition has been successfully applied to automatic defect detection  of  insulators  during  transmission  line  inspections.  Furthermore,  time-series forecasting models are widely used for load prediction and equipment remaining useful life  estimation.  These  successful  applications  provide  methodological  references  and validate the technical feasibility for intelligent transformer monitoring. Researchers have attempted to utilise  models  such  as  deep belief  networks  (DBN) (Ghosal  et  al.,  2025), convolutional neural networks  (CNN), and long short-term  memory  (LSTM)  to automatically  learn  fault  features  from  massive  monitoring  data,  thereby  reducing reliance  on  human  expertise  to  a  certain  extent  (Xue  et  al.,  2007).  For  instance,  some studies  employ  CNNs  to  analyse  drain  gas  analysis  (DGA)  data,  identifying  complex nonlinear relationships between gas content and fault modes (Jiang et al., 2011). Other researchers utilise LSTMs to process time-series data like transformer vibration signals, capturing their dynamic characteristics. However, these deep learning models based on single  data  sources  remain  inadequate  when  confronting  the  complex  challenges  of real-world  engineering  (Agrawal  et  al.,  2024).  The  primary  challenge  is  the  data bottleneck: acquiring high-quality fault samples is difficult, leading to severely imbalanced datasets (e.g., far more normal-state samples than fault samples). Simultaneously,  data  annotation  is  costly  and  inevitably  contaminated  by  uncertainties such as measurement noise and environmental interference (Favela et al., 2010). Second, models suffer from insufficient interpretability and generalisation capabilities: most deep learning models operate like 'black boxes (Etin et al., 2024),' making their decision-making  processes  difficult  for  operations  personnel  to  understand  and  trust. Furthermore,  models  trained  on  a  specific  dataset  may  exhibit  significant  performance degradation when applied to transformers of different models or operating environments (Mondal and Kumbhar, 2017).

To  overcome  these  limitations,  current  research  is  advancing  toward  multi-source information  fusion,  few-shot  learning,  and  model  lightweighting  (Sun  et  al.,  2025). Multi-source fusion is a key pathway to enhancing diagnostic reliability (Ciampi et al., 2005). Single-source DGA data or vibration signals may fail to comprehensively reflect a device's health status (Si et al., 2024). Therefore, integrating multi-source information such as electrical quantities (current, voltage), vibration signals, acoustic signals, infrared thermal imaging, and even equipment logs and maintenance histories - to build a more comprehensive condition awareness system has become a significant trend. For instance, research  has  proposed  integrating  machine  vision  with  auditory  responses  to  locate discharge  defects  via  acoustic  imaging  (Langers  et  al.,  2005).  By  utilising  CNN  to identify acoustic signal features, this approach achieves an 87.51% recognition accuracy even  in  noisy  environments.  Additionally,  studies  in  the  regulation  domain  have developed transformer situational awareness and early warning models through correlation  mining  of  alarm  information  (Sebastian,  2011),  defect  records,  and  online monitoring data. Addressing data scarcity, frameworks like active learning and reinforcement learning demonstrate significant potential (Fang† et al., 2014). One study proposed  an  enhanced  active learning-deep neural network  fusion algorithm that intelligently selects the most valuable samples for annotation (Star, 2001), substantially improving learning efficiency and fault identification accuracy under small and imbalanced sample conditions. Meanwhile, reinforcement learning addresses the trade-off  between  response  speed  and  diagnostic  accuracy  in  protection  systems  (Teng and Tan, 2008). For instance, one framework models transformer differential protection as  a  markov  decision  process  (Jazebi  et  al.,  2009),  enabling  adaptive  data  length adjustment (Choi et al., 2009). This approach substantially reduces response time while maintaining high precision (Enderlin et al., 2013). These explorations provide valuable insights for developing more data-efficient and environment-adaptive intelligent diagnostic models (Yu et al., 2007).

Despite  significant  progress  in  existing  research,  developing  a  truly  robust  (Walsh and  Warren,  1982),  practical,  and  reliable  intelligent  diagnostic  system  for  power transformers still faces numerous challenges. First, at the multimodal data fusion level, a key  scientific  question  is  how  to  design  an  effective  architecture  that  collaboratively processes  vastly  different  heterogeneous  data  (such  as  static  DGA  data  and  dynamic vibration  time-series  signals)  while  adaptively  balancing  the  contributions  of  different data  sources  (Hou  et  al.,  2025),  rather  than  simply  concatenating  them.  Second,  at  the model training level, ensuring that models remain sensitive to the majority class samples while  accurately  identifying  rare  early-stage  fault  signs  -  preventing  false  negatives  under  extremely  imbalanced  data  distributions  (e.g.,  where  severe  fault  samples  are scarce)  remains  a  major  challenge  (Ye  et  al.,  2021).  Finally,  and  currently  a  relatively weak area of research, lies enhancing the interpretability of the model's decision-making process. This would enable maintenance personnel to understand the model's 'reasoning logic (Flynn et al., 2013),' thereby building confidence in human-machine collaborative decision-making. This research addresses these challenges by exploring a novel solution to  enhance  the  accuracy  (Lithgow  et  al.,  2017),  robustness,  and  engineering  utility  of power transformer condition monitoring and fault diagnosis (Rigatos and Siano, 2016).

## 2 Related work

Before the rise of deep learning, algorithms like SVM  and random forests gained  popularity  for  such  tasks  due  to  their  strong  generalisation  performance  on small-to-medium-sized  datasets,  relatively  low  computational  cost,  and  a  degree  of interpretability  for  high-dimensional  features.  Deep  learning  technology  enables  the automatic learning of hierarchical feature representations from raw data by constructing neural networks with multiple hidden layers, providing a powerful paradigm for power transformer fault diagnosis. This chapter systematically elaborates on the core theoretical foundations underlying the methodology presented herein.

## 2.4 Multimodal fusion and transformer fault diagnosis

Power transformer fault diagnosis is fundamentally a problem of multi-source information perception. DGA data provides chemical evidence of insulation degradation, whilst  vibration  signals  reflect  physical  changes  in  mechanical  condition.  Traditional approaches predominantly process these two information types independently, failing to fully  exploit  their  complementary  nature.  In  recent  years,  researchers  have  begun exploring  multimodal  deep  learning  architectures;  however,  how  to  effectively  fuse heterogeneous  data  sources  and  adaptively  balance  contributions  from  each  modality remains  a  critical  issue  requiring  resolution.  The  proposed  CNN-BiLSTM-Attention framework  addresses  precisely  this  challenge,  enabling  the  collaborative  perception  of DGA local features and vibration temporal dynamics.

## 4 Experimental verification

## 4.1 Experimental setup and dataset description

To comprehensively evaluate the performance of the proposed CNN-BiLSTM hybrid model with multi-head attention mechanism (hereafter referred to as CNN-BiLSTM-attention),  experiments  were  conducted  using  two  publicly  available authoritative  datasets.  The  IEC  TC  10  DGA  dataset  and  the  IEEE  PES  Transformer Vibration  Dataset  were  selected  for  this  evaluation  as  they  are  widely  recognised benchmark datasets within the community. Their public availability ensures reproducibility,  and  their  coverage  of  a  comprehensive  range  of  states  -  from  normal operation to various typical faults - provides a reliable foundation for a fair and thorough assessment of diagnostic algorithm performance. The first dataset, sourced from the IEC TC 10 database,  comprises  287  DGA  samples  from  multiple  operational  transformers. Each sample contains five key gas concentrations: C2H2/C2H4, CH4/H2, C2H4/C2H6 gas concentrations. Samples are labeled according to the IEC 60599 standard with six states: normal, low-energy discharge (D1), high-energy discharge (D2), local overheating (T1), medium  overheating  (T2),  and  high  overheating  (T3).  The  second  dataset  is  the transformer vibration dataset provided by institute of electrical and electronics engineers PES.  This  dataset  was  collected  from  vibration  acceleration  signals  on  the  surfaces  of multiple 500 kV transformer tanks, sampled at 10 kHz. Each sample contains 2,048 data points and is labelled with corresponding fault types.

Before experimentation, the data underwent rigorous pre-processing. The DGA data was  z-score  normalised  according  to  formula  in  this  paper.  Z-score  normalisation  was chosen over alternatives like min-max normalisation primarily because it better preserves the  shape  of  the  original  data  distribution  and  is  less  sensitive  to  potential  outliers, thereby enhancing model robustness in real-world noisy environments. Vibration signals were first denoised using a Butterworth low-pass filter with a cutoff frequency of 2 kHz. Then,  time-domain  features  (root  mean  square,  peak  value,  kurtosis,  waveform  factor) and frequency-domain features (amplitude of the top 10 dominant frequency components) were calculated for each signal segment (2,048 points in length), forming a 14-dimensional  feature  vector  that  was  similarly  normalised.  Finally,  through  sample time  alignment,  a  multimodal  dataset  comprising  287  samples  is  constructed.  Each sample  contains  5-dimensional  DGA  data  and  14-dimensional  vibration  features.  The dataset is randomly split into a training set (200 samples) and a test set (87 samples) at a 7:3 ratio. To mitigate the class imbalance issue, SMOTE oversampling is applied to the minority class samples in the training set.

The comparative baseline for this experiment selected four representative methods in the field:

- Traditional SVM model: support vector machines employing radial basis function (RBF) kernels, with feature inputs comprising manually selected DGA ratios. These baseline models were chosen as they represent key methodological milestones in the evolution of fault diagnosis: from traditional statistical machine learning (SVM), to shallow deep learning (DBN), and then to modern deep learning models specialised in static feature extraction (CNN) and sequential modelling (BiLSTM). Comparing against them effectively frames the proposed model's position and contribution within this technical progression. This approach replicates the classical methodology from reference.
- DBN: a DBN model with three hidden layers is employed for fault classification. Standard 1D CNN model: a four-layer convolutional-pooling architecture processes DGA data.
- BiLSTM model: a two-layer BiLSTM network processes vibration feature sequences.

All  deep  learning  models  employ  the  ADAM  optimiser,  with  an  initial  learning rate  of  0.001,  a  batch  size  of  16,  and  a  training  cycle  of  200.  in  the  proposed CNN-BiLSTM-attention model, the CNN branch employs two convolutional layers (with 32 and 64 filters, respectively), the BiLSTM branch has 64 hidden units, and the attention head count is set  to  4.  Evaluation  metrics  include  accuracy,  precision,  recall,  f1-score, and macro area under the ROC curve (AUC).

## 4.2 Overall performance comparison and analysis

To fairly compare the overall performance of all models on transformer fault diagnosis tasks, we ran each comparison algorithm and the proposed model on the same test set, calculating  macro-average  precision,  recall,  F1  score,  and  accuracy.  The  results  are shown  in  Table  2.  The  proposed  CNN-BiLSTM-Attention  model  achieved  the  best results  across  all  four  metrics,  with  an  accuracy  of  98.2%  and  an  F1  score  of  97.8%, significantly  outperforming  other  comparison  models.  The  traditional  SVM  model performed the worst due to its reliance on manually defined ratio features and difficulty in  capturing  complex  nonlinear  relationships.  The  DBN  model  outperformed  SVM, demonstrating  the  effectiveness  of  deep  feature  learning.  However,  its  unsupervised pre-training process may not be optimal for the data scale of this task. Standard CNN and BiLSTM models excel at processing DGA data and vibration sequences, respectively, but their performance bottlenecks arise from relying solely on single-modal information. The proposed  model  achieves significant performance  improvements  through  effective multimodal fusion and attention mechanisms.

To comprehensively evaluate the classification performance of the models, we plotted the macro-averaged  ROC  curves  for  all  models,  as  shown  in  Figure  2.  The  ROC  curve depicts how the true positive rate (TPR) varies with the false positive rate (FPR) across all possible classification thresholds. The closer the area under the curve (AUC) is to 1, the  better  the  model  performance. The figure clearly shows that the ROC curve of the proposed model is closest to the upper-left corner, achieving an AUC value of 0.994 significantly higher than other comparison models. This demonstrates the superior overall classification  performance  of the proposed  model,  particularly in balancing fault detection with false alarm avoidance.

## 4.3 Ablation experiments and model analysis

To  validate  the  actual  contributions  of  each  core  component  proposed  in  this  paper (multimodal  fusion,  attention  mechanism),  we  designed  rigorous  ablation  experiments. We  constructed  three  variant  models:  w/o  BiLSTM:  only  the  CNN  branch  processes DGA data, removing vibration signal input and the BiLSTM branch. w/o CNN: only the BiLSTM  branch  processes  vibration  data,  removing  DGA  data  input  and  the  CNN branch.  w/o  attention:  retains  both  CNN  and  BiLSTM  branches  but  removes  the multi-head  attention  fusion  module,  instead  performing  simple  feature  concatenation before  direct  input  to  the  classifier.  All  variant  models  were  trained  and  tested  under identical conditions.

As shown in Figure 3, which evaluates the experimental results using accuracy and F1 score,  the  removal  of  any  single  component  degrades  the  model's  performance.  The performance of both single-modal models (w/o BiLSTM and w/o CNN) falls below that of the complete model, fully demonstrating the effectiveness of the multimodal learning strategy  that  integrates  DGA  and  vibration  information.  The  two  data  sources  exhibit complementary  characteristics.  Furthermore,  the  significant  performance  drop  after removing  the  attention  mechanism  (w/o  attention)  -  with  accuracy  decreasing  from 98.2%  to  95.5%  -  highlights  the  critical  role  of  attention  in  adaptively  weighting  key features and enhancing the model's discriminative capability.

To  further explore the model's  internal  decision-making  mechanism,  we  used  a high-energy discharge sample as an example and plotted the model's attention weight bar charts  for  each  input  feature,  as  shown  in  Figure  4.  The  height  of  each  bar  directly represents the magnitude of the weight assigned to that feature. It is clearly observable that the model assigns the highest attention weights to acetylene (C 2H2) gas content and specific  frequency  components  of  the  vibration  signal  (e.g.,  frequency  2).  This  aligns perfectly  with  the  physical  mechanism  where  high-energy  discharge  faults  generate significant  amounts  of  acetylene  gas  and  induce  mechanical  vibrations  at  specific frequencies. This visualisation provides interpretability for the model, helping maintenance  personnel  understand  the  diagnostic  rationale  and  enhancing  trust  in  the intelligent  diagnostic  system. ## 4.4 Statistical significance test

To ensure the reliability of the performance improvement, we conducted a paired t-test on the F1 scores between our proposed model and the baseline model. The hypothesis test was set as follows: the null hypothesis H 0 states that there is no significant difference in performance  between  the  two  models;  the  alternative  hypothesis H 1 states  that  our proposed  model  significantly  outperforms  the  baseline  model.  We  randomly  split  the training/test  sets  and  repeated  the  experiment  30  times,  yielding  30  pairs  of  F1  score observations. The calculated t-statistic value was 5.87, far exceeding the critical value at the significance level α =  0.01 (with 29 degrees of freedom), yielding a p-value below 0.0001. Therefore, we reject the null hypothesis with 99% confidence, concluding that the proposed CNN-BiLSTM-Attention model indeed demonstrates a statistically significant performance improvement.

## 5 Conclusions

This paper proposes a deep learning model for power transformer condition monitoring and fault diagnosis. The model incorporates CNN, bidirectional LSTM, and a multi-head attention mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that this model achieves significantly  superior  performance  compared  to  traditional  methods  on  both  the  public IEC dataset and transformer vibration datasets, with an average diagnostic accuracy of 98.2%  and  an  F1  score  of  97.8%.  Compared  to  the  best-performing  baseline  model BiLSTM,  accuracy  improved  by  5.1  percentage  points;  compared  to  traditional  SVM methods, the improvement exceeded 13 percentage points. Ablation experiments further confirm that the synergistic fusion of multimodal data (DGA and vibration signals) and the  adaptive  weighting  of  key  features  via  the  attention  mechanism  are  the  two  core contributors  to  the  model's  performance  improvement,  yielding  approximately  3%  and 2.7% accuracy gains, respectively. Moreover, through attention weight visualisation, the model  demonstrates  strong  interpretability. It clearly indicates key  features (e.g., acetylene gas content, specific vibration frequency bands) highly correlated with specific faults  (such  as  high-energy  discharges).  This  provides  maintenance  personnel  with intuitive evidence to understand and trust the model's diagnostic decisions.

The theoretical contributions of this study primarily manifest at the methodological level.  First,  we  successfully  constructed  an  effective  heterogeneous  information  fusion framework,  resolving  the  challenge  of  synergistically  processing  static  DGA  data  and dynamic vibration sequences. This provides novel insights for applying multi-source data in equipment condition monitoring. Second, introducing attention mechanisms into fault diagnosis not only enhances model performance but, more importantly, paves a feasible path toward improving the interpretability of deep learning models, advancing the shift from 'black-box' to 'white-box' understanding. Finally, addressing the widespread issue of class imbalance in practical engineering, the combined design of label smoothing and focal  loss  loss  functions  proves  effective,  delivering  a  practical  technical  solution  for small-sample fault diagnosis.
